public_notes.title: A Community Name With A Longer History
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history connects Passaunkack with the area of today's Upper Mattaponi community. It describes Upper Mattaponi participation in the 1677 Treaty of Middle Plantation under Cockacoeske, then an Adamstown community recorded in 1885 and the adoption of the Upper Mattaponi Tribe name in 1921. This is the Tribe's historical account, not a present land-boundary or treaty-rights determination.

public_notes.title: Sharon Indian School And Community Continuity
public_notes.text: The school history dates construction to 1919, closure to 1965 and King William County's return of the building to the Tribe to 1987. The About page distinguishes an earlier school from a 1950s replacement. The Tribe's pages describe the school as a gathering place and the Foundation as a steward of its history and educational work. These are the publisher's accounts; they do not establish today's access, hours, staffing or program results.

public_notes.title: River Homelands And Displacement
public_notes.text: The Nation's history describes Nansemond settlements along both sides of the river and membership in the Tsenacomoco, or Powhatan, coalition. It recounts English displacement during the Anglo-Powhatan Wars of 1610 to 1646 and differing family responses to colonial pressure. The account emphasizes that political differences did not end family and kinship ties. This is its historical account, not a present land-boundary determination.

public_notes.title: Community Institutions And Self-Government
public_notes.text: The Nation describes an Indiana Methodist Church established around 1850 for the Nansemond community in Norfolk County. Its history says the same site later housed a public school for Nansemond children in the 1890s. It dates formal organization with elected officers to 1984 and explains its return to the name Nansemond Indian Nation. These are connected parts of the Nation's account of community continuity.
